tier_reason: First-party README tables. The only same-session comparison is the 4 vCPU Xeon Skylake VM table (2026-09, Mojo 1.0.0, llama2.c OpenMP 4 threads vs llama2.mojo -j 4 and both single-threaded; best of 3 and byte-identical greedy output per agents-optimization.md), with the llama2.c compiler, flags and commit unstated, so C. The headline M1 Max table is a cross-run comparison: README history (3c556c3, f6ce354 vs 0baf4d4) shows the llama2.c and llama.cpp columns unchanged since the Nov 2023 6-thread run while only the Mojo column was re-measured in 2026 with 8 workers.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README (last run 2026-09-12, Mojo 1.0.0, PR #102 build). Same-session 4 vCPU Intel Xeon Skylake AVX-512 VM: llama2.c OpenMP 4 threads 292/117/53/5.2 tok/s vs llama2.mojo -j 4 327/150/66/6.8 for stories15M/42M/110M/TinyLlama-1.1B (1.12x/1.28x/1.25x/1.31x, derived from page data); single-threaded llama2.c 105/40/16/1.7 vs llama2.mojo -j 1 154/54/22 (1.35-1.47x, derived from page data). upgradelog.md reports another run of the same build at -j 4 400/159/58 and -j 1 143/51/21 against the same llama2.c figures, and the author states +-10% run-to-run noise with both sides at the VM's ~20 GB/s memory-bandwidth ceiling. The Mac M1 Max table (llama2.mojo 1283/506/218 tok/s with 8 workers vs llama2.c 730/270/102 and llama.cpp 890/420/187) pairs a 2026 Mojo run with llama2.c and llama.cpp figures carried over unchanged from the Nov 2023 README (then labelled 6 threads, Mojo 1025/490/195), so its 1.8-2.1x ratio is cross-run. i7-8700 (2023 run): parity, 440 vs 435, 63 vs 64 and 7.25 vs 7.25 tok/s. The headline 'outperforms llama2.c by 30% ... llama.cpp by 20%' dates from the 2023 M1 Max figures.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Mojo 1.0.0 (Modular 26.5) for the 2026-09 runs (the README now targets Mojo 1.1.0, whose threading change was not re-benchmarked); llama2.c compiler, flags and commit not stated for any table (upstream 'make runomp' is gcc -Ofast -fopenmp -march=native); llama.cpp version, build and model format not stated.
corrections.hardware: Apple M1 Max (Mojo column 2026 with 8 workers; llama2.c and llama.cpp columns from a Nov 2023 run with 6 threads); 4 vCPU Intel Xeon Skylake AVX-512 VM, Ubuntu 26.04 (same-session 2026 table); Intel Core i7-8700 3.2 GHz, Ubuntu 20.04 (2023 table).
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers. The M1 Max headline table is a cross-run comparison: the llama2.c and llama.cpp columns are the Nov 2023 figures (6 threads) left unchanged when only the Mojo column was re-measured on 2026-09-12 with 8 workers, so its 1.8-2.1x ratio and the llama.cpp comparison are not valid evidence; the 2023 i7-8700 table shows parity. The valid same-session evidence is the Xeon Skylake 4 vCPU VM table: 1.12-1.31x at 4 threads (the author notes both sides sit at the VM's ~20 GB/s memory-bandwidth ceiling with +-10% noise, and another run in upgradelog.md shows 400 vs 292 tok/s on stories15M) and 1.35-1.47x single-threaded, with the llama2.c compiler, flags and commit unstated. Greedy output is byte-identical to llama2.c, so the work is the same. The multi-thread win comes from a persistent spin-barrier worker pool (31 barriers per token, per-worker redundant RMSNorm) against llama2.c's per-call OpenMP parallel for, and the single-thread win from tuned SIMD tiling (nelts), both reproducible in C; the optimisation was done by coding agents (agents-optimization.md). The Mojo 1.1 update (2026-09-19) replaced the TaskGroup pool with one max.algorithm.parallelize dispatch per forward pass and was not re-benchmarked. The linked engiware.com M1 Max comparison does not resolve (DNS failure) and arXiv 2502.01651 is blocked here, so no independent numbers were read.
corrections.why_faster: Implementation choices rather than the language: a persistent worker pool with spin barriers (31 per token on stories15M) and per-worker redundant RMSNorm instead of llama2.c's OpenMP fork-join per matmul, plus an explicit SIMD matmul with tuned nelts = max(16, simd_width); llama2.c relies on compiler auto-vectorisation of a naive loop. At 4 threads both sides are memory-bandwidth bound on the VM.

notes: Keep at C, but stop quoting the M1 Max 1.8-2.1x and the 'llama.cpp by 20%' line: they compare a 2026 Mojo run (8 workers) with 2023 llama2.c/llama.cpp figures (6 threads). Valid evidence is the Xeon VM table, 1.12-1.31x at 4 threads (near the author's stated +-10% noise on stories15M) and 1.35-1.47x single-threaded, with llama2.c flags unstated; the win comes from threading and tiling design, not Mojo itself, and the current Mojo 1.1 code was not re-benchmarked.

tier_reason: Upgraded C to A: the README Performance section names both programs (llama2.zig src/main.zig, which prints its own tok/s, and llama2.c run.c), the exact run commands, the C build (gcc -Ofast -march=native via the quoted Makefile, plus an -O3 -march=native row), the Zig build (zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast, Zig 0.11.0-dev.4315+f5239677e) and the CPU (AMD Ryzen 9 5900X); only the gcc version is missing, which the pdqsort precedent accepts as A. Both programs start the timer after the first token and divide pos-1 tokens by elapsed time, so the tok/s figures are computed the same way.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README, single-threaded, stories15M, 256 tokens, AMD Ryzen 9 5900X: argmax (temperature 0) llama2.zig 660 tok/s vs llama2.c 'make runfast -march=native' (gcc -Ofast) 548 (1.20x, derived from page data) and vs llama2.c 'make run -march=native' (-O3, no fast-math) 122; top-p 0.9 at temperature 1.0: 579 vs 463 (1.25x, derived from page data). Multi-threaded llama2.c 'make runomp' reaches 1564 tok/s (2.4x the single-threaded llama2.zig, derived from page data); llama2.zig has no multithreading. The README Todo says llama2.zig is slower than llama2.c on very small (~100K-parameter) models.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: llama2.zig: Zig 0.11.0-dev.4315+f5239677e, zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast, native target, @setFloatMode(Optimized) in src/main.zig; llama2.c: gcc (version unstated) -Ofast -march=native ('make runfast' with -march=native added, Makefile quoted in the README), plus an -O3 -march=native row.
corrections.caveats: First-party 2023 numbers on one CPU, single runs, gcc version unstated and neither the llama2.c nor the llama2.zig commit pinned (the figures predate the 2024 Zig 0.12/0.14 ports). The Aug 2, 2026 commits were not only CI: they changed the hot path (independent matmul accumulators, attention sums in registers, vectorised RMSNorm, Zig 0.16 port) without re-running the README benchmark, and the current matmul uses 8 or 4 independent vector accumulators, a different accumulator structure from llama2.c's loop; the measured 2023 code (9b225a2) used one vector accumulator per output row. Both sides of the -Ofast row are fast-math builds for the native ISA; the 5x gap to the -O3 row is not a fair comparison because without -ffast-math gcc cannot vectorise the dot-product reduction. The 20-25% win comes from explicit @Vector SIMD, comptime-fused q/k/v and w1/w3 matmuls sharing loads of x, and SIMD-aligned allocation, all doable in C with intrinsics. The README Todo says llama2.c is faster on ~100K-parameter models (expf cost; GCC much better than clang there), and llama2.c's OpenMP build is 2.4x faster than single-threaded llama2.zig.
corrections.why_faster: Explicit SIMD via Zig @Vector in matmul, RMSNorm, softmax and attention (the README credits the SIMD matmul alone with 115 to 430 tok/s within llama2.zig), comptime-generated fused matmuls that compute q/k/v and w1/w3 in one pass over x, and SIMD-aligned allocations, against gcc -Ofast auto-vectorisation of llama2.c's naive matmul loop. Hand-vectorisation and fusion, not a Zig codegen advantage.

notes: Upgraded to A on the pdqsort precedent (gcc named without a version, flags, CPU and code public); cap at C instead if pinned commits are required, since the 2023 commits measured are not named and the hot path changed on 2026-08-02 without a rerun. Shortcomings: one CPU and single 2023 runs, win from hand SIMD and matmul fusion rather than the language, slower than llama2.c on tiny models per the README Todo, no multithreading (llama2.c OpenMP 2.4x faster).

tier_reason: The README at benchmark_url holds only qualitative summary text, but the linked SciMLBenchmarksOutput pages carry work-precision plots from public jmd code with Julia 1.11.9, package versions (Sundials.jl v6.7.1, Sundials_jll v7.5.0+0) and the CPU (AMD EPYC 7502) in each appendix. The C solvers are BinaryBuilder Sundials_jll builds with no compiler or flags stated and the suite is run by the SciML project on its own solvers, so first-party C, not A or B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: SciMLBenchmarks README summary (no numbers): non-stiff 'OrdinaryDiffEq.jl's methods are the most efficient by a good amount', the Vern methods do best, ARKODE and Hairer dopri5/dop853 are 'far less efficient than the Vern methods', CVODE_Adams and lsoda 'tend to not do very well'; stiff: ARKODE is inconsistent and KenCarp4 is 'much more efficient in most cases'. Rigid Body work-precision plot (RigidBody_wpd_5_1, 3 equations, AMD EPYC 7502): Vern7/Vern8 take about 2e-5 to 1e-4 s while CVODE_Adams and ARKODE (explicit, order 6) take about 1e-4 to 1e-3 s over the same error range, roughly 5-10x at matched error (read off the plot, derived from page data). On the stiff Pollution page (20 equations) FBDF is only modestly ahead of CVODE_BDF in the high-tolerance plot, and the page's own conclusion reads 'Sundials CVODE_BDF the best here'.
corrections.hardware: AMD EPYC 7502 32-Core (128 threads), Linux; Julia 1.11.9, LLVM 16.0.6 (znver2), per the RigidBody and Pollution page appendices
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.11.9 (LLVM 16.0.6, znver2) for OrdinaryDiffEq; Sundials C library via Sundials.jl v6.7.1 and Sundials_jll v7.5.0+0 (BinaryBuilder build, compiler and flags not stated); ODEInterface_jll v0.0.2 and LSODA_jll v0.1.2 for the secondary baselines
corrections.caveats: First-party suite run by the SciML project on its own solvers. Algorithm versus algorithm: Vern7/8/9 and Tsit5 against Dormand-Prince, Adams and ARKODE methods, so the win is not the language's (same_algorithm false). In this harness the Sundials C solvers are driven through Sundials.jl wrappers with a Julia right-hand side called back across the C boundary on every function evaluation, and each timed solve includes wrapper setup; on 3-equation problems solved in 20 microseconds to 1 ms this fixed overhead weighs heavily, and the Julia methods also get a StaticArrays out-of-place variant (prob_choice 2) that the C library cannot use. Numbers exist only as plots; the RigidBody page notes that some of the gap depends on each library's error norm. The win is not universal: on the stiff Pollution problem the page's conclusion names Sundials CVODE_BDF the best, and FBDF is only modestly ahead in its high-tolerance plot. Fortran baselines (dopri5, dop853, radau, ODEInterface) are out of scope for a C/C++ baseline.
corrections.why_faster: Different integrators (high-order Verner and Tsitouras pairs with cheap interpolants against Dormand-Prince, Adams and ARK methods), type-specialised inlined right-hand sides compiled by Julia, and a harness in which the C solvers pay Julia-to-C callback and wrapper setup costs on every solve.

notes: Keep at C as an algorithm win, not a language win (same_algorithm false, language_level_claim false); benchmark_url moved to the RigidBody output page, which has the plots and the hardware appendix. Shortcomings: first-party, numbers only in plots, C solvers driven through Julia callbacks with wrapper setup inside the timing, Sundials_jll build flags unstated, and the Pollution page names CVODE_BDF the best.
